figures: 1. Figure 1: Runtime speedup from strategic layer dropout. Left: speedup by configuration. Right: scaling with batch size. Strategic dropout achieves 1.28× average speedup, approaching theoretical 1.33× maximum at larger batches.
2. Figure 2: Information flow through transformer layers. Theoretical framework (solid lines) aligns with empirical measurements (points), showing phase transitions at layers 3 and 8.
3. Figure 3: Gradient dynamics showing 1.83× amplification at transition layers (left) and cross-architecture correlation vector to BERT baseline averaging 69.3% (right).

4. Figure 4: Detailed layer-wise vulnerability heatmap across all models showing consistent transitions at layers 3 and 8 in 12-layer architectures (marked with dashed lines). Color intensity represents vulnerability score (0=robust, 1=vulnerable).
5. Figure 5: Comprehensive robustness evaluation across six noise types and five models showing performance degradation patterns. RoBERTa maintains superior robustness across all conditions.
6. Figure 6: Real-world noise impact comparison. Left: Model performance on different real-world noise sources. Right: Systematic gap between synthetic and real-world noise challenges.
results_section: 1. Character-level noise shows moderate impact (average 75.1% robustness retained), while syntactic disruption causes most significant damage (average 54.8% robustness retained).
2. The first phase, spanning layers 0–3, focuses on surface feature extraction, retaining 79% robustness averaged across all noise types.
3. The middle phase from layers 3–8 handles syntactic processing, showing 52% robustness under syntactic noise (65% average across all noise types).
4. The final phase in layers 8–12 performs semantic encoding, maintaining 67% robustness as the model leverages redundant semantic representations.
5. Strategic dropout targeting non-transition layers (dropping layers 1, 5, and 10) achieves 1.28× measured speedup compared to the theoretical maximum of 1.33× for 25% layer removal.
6. Random 25% dropout yields only 1.19× speedup while causing 8 percentage points of absolute performance degradation.
7. Aggressive 50% dropout (6 layers) achieves 1.85× speedup but causes 18 percentage points of absolute performance loss.
8. Speedup improves slightly with batch size, reaching 1.31× at batch=32 due to better GPU utilization amortizing fixed overhead costs.

9. OCR Errors (ICDAR 2019 dataset): Common substitutions from 2,000 scanned documents reduce BERT robustness score from 0.640 (its average robustness on clean synthetic data) to 0.560 (12.5% relative drop).
10. RoBERTa drops from 0.787 to 0.735 (6.6% relative drop) under OCR errors.
11. Character-level denoising before layer 3 recovers 85% of lost performance.
12. Social Media Text: 5,000 tweets with abbreviations and typos cause 18% average degradation, with RoBERTa showing only 8% loss.
13. Adversarial Training improves worst-case robustness by 42% but increases training time 3.5× and inference cost 1.2×.
14. Our method achieves comparable robustness gains (38%) with 1.28× speedup.
15. Certified Defenses provide provable guarantees but reduce clean accuracy by 8-12 percentage points.
16. Knowledge Distillation: DistilBERT achieves 1.6× speedup but shows 18% greater vulnerability to noise.
17. Structured Pruning removes 40% of parameters with 5% accuracy loss but increases noise vulnerability by 23%.
18. Removing layer-wise analysis causes a dramatic 73% drop in detection accuracy.
19. Excluding noise diversity reduces detection accuracy by 61%.
20. Operating without proper statistical validation increases the false positive rate by 34%.
21. Combining layer-wise and noise-type analysis yields a 127% improvement in detection capability.
